key_insight: Fewer than 2% of FDA‑authorized AI medical devices are prognostic, with prediction horizons ranging from minutes to years — revealing a growing but underregulated class of tools that raises unique regulatory and ethical issues.
problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes the scarcity and diversity of prognostic AI devices among FDA approvals and highlights the urgent need to address regulatory and ethical gaps as prognostic tools become more common.
method: Systematic review and classification of FDA‑authorized AI medical devices to identify prognostic vs. non‑prognostic tools
Mapping of prediction horizons (minutes to years) and categorization by clinical application and regulatory pathway
Assessment of regulatory and ethical challenges arising from prognostic use cases
impact: Alerts AI/ML practitioners that prognostic models face distinct validation, transparency, and governance requirements; encourages early incorporation of regulatory strategy, long‑term validation, and ethical safeguards into model design.
visual_elements: Pie chart showing proportion of prognostic vs. non‑prognostic FDA‑authorized AI devices (<2% slice)
Horizontal bar or timeline visualizing range of prediction horizons (minutes → years) with example use cases
Flowchart of regulatory pathway considerations for prognostic devices (validation, monitoring, update controls)
Icon set highlighting key ethical issues: risk stratification, actionability, patient autonomy, and long‑term safety
paper_title: Authorization of prognostic AI medical devices
paper_authors: Urs J. Muehlematter, Kerstin Noelle Vokinger
